The rules of this workbench

You build the connections. The simulation checks those connections using these rules:

  1. A wire joins two terminals. Wires on the same electrical connection may share a trunk; a dot marks a joined branch. A hop marks a crossing without a connection. Use the same terminal to create a branch.
  2. A closed switch joins its two ends. An open switch does not.
  3. The battery provides two different terminal levels, + and −.
  4. The lamp glows when its two ends connect to different battery terminals through wires and closed contacts.
  5. A route directly from + to − that avoids the lamp is a short. The model cuts power and reports it.

The switch contact and lamp filament are drawn inside their parts. They are the starting physical assumptions. There is no hidden AND gate, adder, or completed circuit.

This is an ideal connectivity model for one battery, one lamp, and switches. It does not calculate current, resistance, brightness, component ratings, or real hardware safety.

After these experiments, continue with the original RV8GR hardware labs or Thai module tutorial.

Controls

Add parts from the tray. Drag from one round terminal to another to draw a wire; the target highlights when it will connect. You can also click the two terminals, or focus each terminal and press Enter. Escape cancels a wire or drag. Drag anywhere on a component’s body to move it, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Select a wire or component and press Backspace or Delete to remove it. Undo restores the part and its wires. Text editing keeps its normal keyboard controls.

The input row shows the switch positions currently on the board. Choose the inputs for your next test, make a prediction, then apply the test. Recorded evidence keeps the inputs, prediction, and result from that moment. A correct circuit can still surprise your prediction.
